cls: Fat-soluble vitamin - coagulation factor cofactor (vitamin K-dependent clotting factor synthesis)
pharm: Antihemorrhagic vitamin / vitamin K antagonist reversal agent
quick: Anticoagulant reversal 2.5-10 mg PO/IV; newborn prophylaxis 0.5-1 mg IM
Oral form absorbed better with food/bile; IV available
Compatible; infant newborn prophylaxis still required
May be ineffective if synthetic liver function is severely impaired
INR/PT, signs of bleeding; observe IV infusion for reactions
summary: Vitamin K1 (phytonadione) is the fat-soluble vitamin required for hepatic synthesis of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X and proteins C and S. It is used to treat and prevent bleeding from vitamin K deficiency, to reverse the anticoagulant effect of warfarin and other vitamin K antagonists, and as routine prophylaxis against vitamin K deficiency bleeding (haemorrhagic disease) of the newborn. Intravenous administration carries a risk of severe anaphylactoid reactions and should be given slowly and only when other routes are unsuitable.
indications: Vitamin K deficiency bleeding prophylaxis in newborns (haemorrhagic disease of the newborn)
Anticoagulant-induced (warfarin / vitamin K antagonist) hypoprothrombinemia and reversal of elevated INR
Hypoprothrombinemia due to malabsorption, obstructive jaundice, biliary fistula, or sprue
Hypoprothrombinemia from drugs interfering with vitamin K (e.g., antibiotics, salicylates)

dosage.n: Within 1 hour of birth (single IM dose); oral regimens are alternatives

dosage.c: Warfarin reversal - high INR, no major bleeding
dosage.n: Low oral dose; recheck INR; aim to avoid over-correction

dosage.d: 5 to 10 mg IV by slow infusion
dosage.n: Give with PCC or FFP for immediate reversal; infuse slowly

admin: Prefer the oral or subcutaneous/IM route; reserve IV for when other routes are not feasible
When IV is necessary, dilute and infuse slowly (not faster than ~1 mg/minute) due to anaphylactoid reaction risk
Onset of effect is not immediate - combine with PCC or fresh frozen plasma for urgent bleeding
Protect from light; oral absorption improves with bile/food
Effect can be antagonized if the patient remains on warfarin
moa: Phytonadione is the fat-soluble form of vitamin K required as a cofactor for the hepatic enzyme gamma-glutamyl carboxylase, which carboxylates glutamate residues on coagulation factors II (prothrombin), VII, IX and X and on anticoagulant proteins C and S, converting them to their biologically active forms. Restoring vitamin K reverses vitamin K antagonist (warfarin) effect by enabling synthesis of functional clotting factors.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to phytonadione or product components
relative: Severe hepatocellular disease (may be ineffective and large doses can worsen liver function)
Intravenous use except when other routes are not feasible (anaphylactoid risk)

preg: Vitamin K1 is acceptable and frequently used during pregnancy when indicated. It does not readily cross the placenta in large amounts, so maternal dosing alone does not reliably prevent neonatal vitamin K deficiency bleeding - the newborn still requires prophylaxis.
lact: Compatible with breastfeeding. Breast milk contains relatively little vitamin K, so exclusively breastfed infants still require routine newborn vitamin K prophylaxis.
renal: No specific renal dose adjustment is required.
hepatic: In severe hepatocellular disease the liver may be unable to synthesize clotting factors even with adequate vitamin K, so phytonadione may be ineffective; repeated large doses are not helpful and may further impair liver function.

major: Warfarin and other vitamin K antagonists (vitamin K reverses/antagonizes their anticoagulant effect - intended for reversal but causes warfarin resistance afterward)
moderate: Orlistat, bile-acid sequestrants, mineral oil (reduce vitamin K absorption)
Broad-spectrum antibiotics (deplete gut vitamin K, may increase requirement)
minor: High-dose vitamin E (may antagonize vitamin K-dependent clotting)
interactions.food: Absorption of oral form improved by dietary fat and bile
interactions.diagnostics: Corrects/affects PT and INR (the basis of monitoring)

common: Injection site pain, swelling or tenderness
serious: Severe anaphylactoid / anaphylaxis-like reactions with IV use (hypotension, shock, cardiac/respiratory arrest, even with proper dilution and rate)
Over-correction causing warfarin resistance in patients needing ongoing anticoagulation
rare: Haemolytic anemia / hyperbilirubinemia in neonates (high doses, G6PD deficiency)
Skin reactions (eczematous, delayed hypersensitivity at injection site)
emergency: Anaphylactoid reaction during/after IV administration (cardiovascular collapse)

monitoring: Prothrombin time / INR to assess response and avoid over-correction
Signs of continued or recurrent bleeding
Close observation for hypersensitivity during and after IV administration
Bilirubin and haemolysis in neonates given higher doses
counsel: This vitamin helps blood to clot and counteracts blood thinners like warfarin
If you take warfarin, do not change vitamin K intake (diet or supplements) without medical advice
Newborns routinely receive a vitamin K injection to prevent serious bleeding - this is recommended
Report bleeding, bruising, or signs of an allergic reaction after an injection
Effect may take hours; severe bleeding also needs other treatments
pk: Improvement in coagulation typically within 1-2 hours (IV) and PT often normalizes by 12-14 hours; oral effect within 6-10 hours
Clotting factor synthesis maximal within hours of dosing
Short plasma presence; effect depends on resynthesis of clotting factors
Effect persists while clotting factors remain functional (typically several days)
Store at room temperature; protect from light (light-sensitive)
pearls: Vitamin K1 (phytonadione) is the preferred form for clinical use; it does not work instantly, so urgent bleeding also needs PCC or FFP
IV administration can cause fatal anaphylactoid reactions - give slowly and only when other routes are unsuitable
Routine newborn prophylaxis prevents vitamin K deficiency bleeding (classic and late forms); breast milk is low in vitamin K
Over-reversal of warfarin causes temporary warfarin resistance - use the lowest effective dose for non-bleeding high INR
Ineffective in severe liver failure because clotting factor synthesis itself is impaired
missed: For ongoing oral therapy, take a missed dose when remembered unless it is nearly time for the next dose, then skip it; do not double up. For single-dose uses (reversal, newborn prophylaxis) dosing is determined clinically rather than on a fixed schedule.
overdose: Excess vitamin K1 in adults has low toxicity but, in a patient on warfarin, over-administration causes prolonged resistance to re-anticoagulation. In neonates, excessive doses can cause haemolysis, hyperbilirubinemia and kernicterus risk. Management is supportive; for patients needing anticoagulation, heparin can bridge until warfarin is again effective.
